claims.text: A controlled aging treatment can introduce coherent nanoprecipitates into refractory high-entropy alloys.
Introducing coherent nanoprecipitates by aging will improve radiation tolerance.
The nanoprecipitates will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
The intervention will preserve engineering practicality.
The starting material is an additively manufactured refractory high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
Elevated-temperature aging below the melting point enables coherent nanoprecipitation without forming deleterious phases.
The radiation-tolerance benefit should occur during helium-ion or neutron irradiation at fusion-relevant operating temperatures.
The aging treatment will produce a uniform distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates in the alloy matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as sinks that trap irradiation-induced point defects and small defect clusters.
Defect trapping by the nanoprecipitates reduces the nucleation and growth of helium bubbles.
Defect trapping by the nanoprecipitates reduces dislocation-loop formation.
Reducing helium bubbles and dislocation loops mitigates irradiation embrittlement and preserves ductility and strength.
After irradiation, aged specimens will have fewer and smaller helium bubbles than unaged specimens.
After irradiation, aged specimens will retain or improve yield strength and ductility relative to unaged specimens.
Excessive precipitate coarsening or phase segregation may reduce the efficacy of the precipitates as defect sinks.
Extreme irradiation fluxes may diminish the radiation-tolerance benefit.
Precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution must be optimized to maximize defect absorption without compromising ductility.
Compositional variations among refractory high-entropy alloys may alter the balance between radiation tolerance and mechanical integrity.
